utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-96-21-T. The case of the Prosecutor against Zejnil Delalic, Zdravko Mucic, Hazim Delic and Esad Landzo. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Are all the accused persons present?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The defendant Landzo is present, your Honour. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): The defendant Zejnil Delalic is present. MR KARABDIC (in interpretation): Hazim Delic is present. MR TAPUSKOVIC (in interpretation): The defendant Zdravko Mucic is present. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. Last Friday, before the close of the -- in fact, shortly after, I would say, the close of the working day, we received a few applications, one jointly by all defendants' counsel, asking for certain procedures to be adopted. Now specifically I mention the joint application to adopt all motions made by each of them, except as otherwise indicated before the Trial Chamber. Actually, I think this is a fairly difficult thing to say, because, although the reasons adduced for adopting these motions are splendid and intended to minimise the wastage of time, and to make things easier for everyone, it is a fairly difficult thing to ask a Trial Chamber to have a blanket approval of motions not already before it. I think it still would not make a lot of difference if, on each occasion any of the defence counsel brought a motion, each of the other counsel is asked whether he adopted it or not, and, if he did not adopt it, that will be the position. Technically, I think it is not in the interests of proper procedure to grant a blanket approval of motions not already before the Trial Chamber. It would appear it is a very easy thing, because it was a unanimous decision of the defence counsel, but that notwithstanding, I do not think this Trial Chamber should adopt that procedure. It is fairly irregular and perhaps might commit the Trial Chamber to accept things which otherwise would not have been the ideal situation. The other matter which perhaps one needs mention again before I call on the prosecution for its opening speech, if it wants to make any, is the question of the Landzo discovery motion. I am sure the prosecution has been served with that motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: And will be able to react to it, so that we can take that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Do you want us to answer to that motion now, your Honour? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, that is what I mean, because the motion is asking that you should give the names and location and places of --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We are now dealing with a discovery motion, the discovery motion with the addresses. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Mrs McHenry, at my side, has been dealing with that question. I will ask her to argue and answer to it, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Will counsel to Landzo move the motion?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond to this, yes, we did file the motion to compel the prosecution to identify the witnesses and give us the names and locations. I do not have the record of the prior status conferences in front of me, but at the prior status conference, I believe that the Tribunal had ordered that these witnesses' locations be given to us, unless they filed for protection. Now, it has been clear at that the prosecution has filed for protection for witnesses B, C, D, E and F, but, as far as the other witnesses that they have not filed for protection of, I believe that the Rules require that they give us the location. Mr Ostberg has informed us that he has made an attempt to talk to these witnesses and that the witnesses have said that they do not wish to talk to us, but, under the Rules of Discovery, it is not the prosecution's position to be the go-between between the defence and the witnesses, that we should, if they are not under the protection of this tribunal, have a right to go and confront those witnesses ourselves and have the same opportunity to visit with them out of these surroundings as the prosecution has had, in a more relaxed atmosphere, and that is the basis of our request, that, according to the status reports before, according to the rulings of this tribunal, the witnesses that they have not requested protection for should be given to us, their names and locations, so that, before the prosecution calls them to the stand, we have an opportunity to discuss with them the same kind of things that the prosecution has discussed with them, outside the presence and outside of the protection of these walls. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Can we have your reaction, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Teresa McHenry for the Office of the Prosecution. Your Honour, the defence of Esad Landzo has had the names of the witnesses for a significant length of time. What they are now seeking is the current home addresses of the witnesses so that they may attempt to contact the witnesses to ask about pre-trial interviews. There is no Order of the Court at a status hearing, or at any other time directing us to provide those addresses, or to seek a protective order, if we did not. After we received the request from the defence, we took it upon ourselves to contact all the witnesses and ask them whether or not they wish to provide their addresses and whether they wish to provide a pre-trial interview. In speaking with the witnesses, the prosecution did not take a position on the matter and did not influence the witnesses one way or the other. Without exception, the witnesses, or their representatives, have explicitly directed us not to reveal their home addresses, and they have also reported, without exception, that they do not wish to have a pre-trial interview with the defence. Indeed, even the asking of the questions frightened many of the witnesses. The prosecution has now done more than what is required. There is no basis under the Rules, under the Statute, under the accused's right to a fair trial, or under any Order of this Court which would require the prosecution to provide home addresses of witnesses, or seek protective orders when it declines to do so. The Rules, in fact, quite sensibly do not contemplate the provision of home addresses to the defence. The Rules explicitly require the prosecution only to provide the names of the witnesses, while under Rule 67, the defence, on the other hand, is required to provide both names and addresses. Similarly, most national systems do not require the provision of home addresses, and there is no reason to think that there is anything that would indicate that the addresses should be presented in this case, especially when the witnesses have explicitly requested that they do not wish to have their addresses provided, nor do they wish to provide pre-trial interviews. The defence will have the right to cross-examine the witnesses at trial, and they are entitled to nothing more. It is the witness' right to choose whether or not to reveal their addresses. To reveal their home addresses against their wishes could endanger the well-being of the witnesses, including jeopardising their right to privacy and even jeopardising the witnesses's safety and that of their family, and the prosecution could no do this. In all frankness, your Honour, to provide witness addresses, where the witness has requested us not to, would ensure that there is no co-operation with the Tribunal in this case, or in any other case. Indeed, it is a basic right of anyone, be it your Honour's, be it we with the prosecution, even the defence attorneys, not to be forced to reveal their home addresses. To expect the witnesses, who have all been severely victimised by these accused, to reveal their home addresses to these accused, or their attorneys, is frankly unthinkable.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we object at this point to the reference of Miss McHenry that these accused have victimised all these witnesses. That has not been proven in this court of law and she should not be allowed to pre-judge them at this point. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you, I think your objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to Rule 69C. It talks about identity of witnesses, the address also, or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, your Honour, we would explicitly state that it does not include the address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: "Identity" would not include the address?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. We would note, for instance, in Rule 67 the defence is specifically asked to provide both the identity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If you look at Rule 67 it talks about names and then also addresses. It does not talk about identity. This word has been used in Rule 69(c). Rule 67 talks about names and then addresses, but here Rule 69(c) uses the word "identity". Now, would the identity be much larger than merely name, or include address also?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would state that there is nothing about the witness' current address which would be included under their identity. It is possible that you could say their birth date, or where they are from, some of those things arguably might, but I do not believe that there is any way that one could argue that the witness' home address could be considered part of their identity. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might briefly respond, what has happened is the defence of Esad Landzo has provided to the prosecution names and addresses of witnesses that we intend to call pursuant to alibi or any defences that we have offered, and, as such, the prosecution has sent investigators out there and interviewed these people in their home environment. Now, what this does, it gives them the opportunity to investigate motives for fabrication, what their position is in their community, all the surrounding circumstances around this witness, because we have not been afforded the same possibility for investigation. The defence case is highly prejudiced in that we cannot go talk to the neighbours, "Is this person known to be a liar?", talk to the people surrounding the circumstances. We have no information when that witness takes this stand to decide whether he is a person who normally tells the truth or not, other than what the prosecution's investigator has said. So we are severely prejudiced in that they now have had the opportunity to interview our witnesses and we have not been afforded the same right. Thank you, your Honour. MR TAPUSKOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honour, I am Tapuskovic from Belgrade. What we heard from our colleague is quite correct. Therefore, I should like to second her position, because, as defence counsel already in January, or even before, in August, I submitted a certain number of names of witnesses who will be called to testify in the defence of Zdravko Mucic, and I counted on the possibility of the prosecution contacting them. For me, this was nothing that I would object to, and, therefore, I think this is another point at which the defence is in an unequal position. Thank you. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honour, may I too support what our colleagues have said, and add by saying that, by disclosure of the addresses of the defendants too, Rule 21 of the Statute is being violated. I think that, under the excuse that the defence may exert certain pressure on the witnesses, one might say that someone else is pressuring those witnesses, and that possibility cannot be excluded. That is why I think, in the interests of a fair trial, the prosecution should be required to submit the addresses of the witnesses to us. MR KARABDIC (in interpretation): As defence counsel of defendant Delic, I would like to support the views of the previous speakers and especially what Madam Residovic has just said. I believe that, by acting in this way, the prosecution is jeopardising the basic rights of the counsel of the defendants to be able to question the witnesses and collect data about them, the more so as the witnesses are in other states in other regions, and the prosecution and others can reach them more easily, which we are unable to do. We cannot talk to them or contact them or collect the basic information about them. MR BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, as defence counsel of Esad Landzo, I should like to ask the prosecution, who are the witnesses afraid of? Is it us, the counsels, and an interview with the counsels, or their investigating Judges? Not one of those witnesses is living on the territory of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They are living either in the territory of the Republika Srpska in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or in third countries. Therefore, this possible fear that the prosecution is referring to is imaginary and non-existent, in fact. We believe for the defence to be in an equitable position, it should have access to the witnesses and be able to have pre-trial interviews with them. All witnesses of the defence are accessible to the prosecution and the prosecution has talked to all the witnesses that it was interested in talking to. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Please, can I ask Miss McHenry, is it one of the arguments that the witnesses have refused that you should disclose their addresses or their identities to anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is one of our arguments. Our first argument is that there is no requirement whatsoever that we do so. In fact, though, in an effort to assist the defence and ensure that we did everything possible, we contacted the witnesses and asked whether or not they objected to us providing their addresses to the defence, and it is the case, and, if a witness agrees that we may turn over the address, we are happy to do so. Thus far, every witness we have contacted has explicitly stated "Do not reveal my address to the defence". JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. MR BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honour, before you rule on this matter, I should like to draw attention to one further point. We would like to have this pre-trial interview before each of the witnesses were to appear before the Trial Chamber, the defence would like to have a pre-trial interview with them, and, in direct contact with the witnesses, we could see whether they wished to talk to defence counsel or not, prior to the actual trial proceedings, therefore allowing the defence to verify the position of the witnesses. So I do not see why witnesses could not have pre-trial interviews immediately before making their statements in the court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Are you not asking for a right which is not available to you under the Rules? Are you not asking for a right which is not available to you under the Rules, that you want to interview the prosecution witnesses, whether they want to talk to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might respond, I do not know that it is so important that we interview the witnesses right here in The Hague before they testify as know their identity and location so that we can investigate them as a person, investigate the circumstances surrounding their lives so that, when they come into this courtroom to testify, we know something about them, other than what the prosecution has told us. It is very important for us to be able to have the same investigative right that the prosecution has had, and that they can go out to their location, they can interview the people that these people work with every single day, and they can find out something about their personal lives, something other than what the prosecution has provided us with, and that is the purpose of needing their identities, more than their actual testimony and an interview with them. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually, it seems to me what the prosecution is protecting is the matter of confidentiality between the prosecution lawyers and their client who is a witness, and it is somewhat of a strict matter in legal proceedings. The confidentiality of this nature ought to be respected.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I respond? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The witnesses that the prosecution has sought protection for we certainly are not going to object if there is a legitimate reason for them to have protection, but that leaves about 35 or 40 other witnesses that they have not sought protection for, and we are asking that it is very important for us to find out the location of these witnesses so that we can send our investigators to have the same advantage that the prosecution investigators have taken advantage of. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: We have had enough of this argument. We will make our rulings later. Now we shall proceed to the opening speeches of the prosecuting counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I believe we have a couple of other motions before the Court before we begin opening statement. One is the joint motion in limine, and the other one would be that we have -- we would like to invoke the rule before the trial begins, the Rule 90(d), I believe, which says that the other witnesses should not be available in the trial chambers, or in the audience, whenever other witnesses are testifying. It is up to the discretion of the Court when you want to hear this matter, of course, but we do have a joint motion in limine that needs to be ruled upon before evidence is given. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Now, please, for the last suggestion you have made about witnesses being out of court and out of hearing, it is a normal tradition of every Tribunal, of every Trial Chamber, and I think that announcement normally would be made when it becomes necessary. What are joint defences, joint motions, I stated it very clearly, that it is a little irregular for one to pre-judge what would be coming up in the future. Whenever the motion is filed, it behoves every defendant's counsel who is interested in it either to associate himself with that motion and adopt it, or state his objection to going it alone without that motion. So you do not have to come by such a joint decision. It is a very excellent thing, you have done that, I accept in the right lines, but definitely it is unnecessary in the interests of justice to gag future motions by adopting a motion in a blanket way meeting everything that would come in the future.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, we agree with you. I believe you are referring to the motion to adopt the other objections of the other defendants, but we have another motion also, which is a motion in limine regarding appropriate terms to be used in trial, and we have objections to terms used by the prosecution that are highly prejudicial under Rule 70(f) that need to be resolved before I believe Mr Ostberg begins his opening statement, and before the reading of the indictment. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: We do not read the indictment again. I think they have pleaded to it. Apart from that, I already appreciate your approach, because much of what you are saying I think need not even come before the Trial Chamber. If somebody is using an inappropriate terminology, you can object to it when it is used, and the Trial Chamber will take cognisance of that objection, and especially when you mention terminologies which are not peculiar, I do not see why anybody should come by way of motion and make it a decision of the Trial Chamber, because you do not want a particular expression to be used. It does not follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Just so that I am clear, since this is all new to me, just whenever these terms are used that we object to, we object and the Court will rule on it? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, you would have indicated to the Prosecutor, or whoever is using that terminology, it is inappropriate, and perhaps you would show reason, but it should not come by way of motion at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honours. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honour, before giving the floor to the prosecution, allow me, in connection with this motion of the defence, to present my view. I think that the Court should take a position on this motion, even though the indictment will not be read, because the indictment is a component part of this trial, it begins with it and it will serve as a basis for presenting to the public everything that is happening in this Trial Chamber. I must say that the decision on this motion is of twofold significance: first, because, before the Court, we have for the first time members of the legal Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, an independent and internationally recognised country with legal bodies and legitimate names, the use of terms such as "Muslim forces", "Muslim courts", the commander of the Muslim forces is absolutely legally unacceptable, and such terms cannot be used in such a lofty institution as this. On behalf of my defendant, I must say that he was never a member of the Muslim forces, nor was he a commander of the Muslim forces. On the other hand, Bosnia and Herzegovina is an independent and sovereign country, with its own institutions, and it would be correct in this court, as is the case in the United Nations, to use those terms which the bodies of Bosnia and Herzegovina actually have, and I think that such a decision should be taken straightaway, and that the prosecution should be asked to correct those terms and to submit such a corrected version of the indictment to this Court. Allow me one further point. I think that these are questions contributing to a fair trial, which is in the interests of the Court and of us, as the defence counsel. From a part of the mass media this morning I learnt of a sensationalist invitation to this trial, whereby this case is being linked to the trials in Nuremberg and Tokyo. I wish to express my deep disagreement with such announcements regarding this case. By presenting numerous evidence, we will seek to prove the innocence of our defendants. We expect a fair trial and such an inappropriate announcement of this case will not contribute to it. I should like also to say that, as a member of the defence team of my defendant, Delalic, I will oppose any attempts which would infringe upon his rights as stipulated by Article 21 of the Statute, and any other tendencies which may undermine the fairness of this trial. I felt it my duty to make this statement before the beginning of the proceedings. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much, Mrs Residovic. We appreciate your contribution, and, as I indicated from the beginning, it is always appropriate for counsel to point out inaccuracies or poor representation of facts or poor misdescriptions of situations to the Trial Chamber for correction, and it is not a thing which can be done once one has tried the whole trial. It can be done as it arises and depending on the situation which confronts you. I do not think the Trial Chamber has any responsibility, whatever adverse publicity you might have read. It is not our duty, except it affects the trial as a whole, to issue any corrections, and I think you should not mind so much of what you have read or heard, but do your best in the interests of your client for the purposes of the justice of the case before the Trial Chamber. We assure you the best from now, and from the beginning, as you have been very familiar with. The Trial Chamber has cooperated with every aspect of this case, both with the prosecution and defence, and there is no reason why you should have any fears from whatever you have heard elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to state that the defence of Esad Landzo would wish to adopt the arguments of Zejnil Delalic at this point also. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually, I have already indicated the view the Trial Chamber takes. It is not necessary for us to rule on such a motion I say once as our decision. Perhaps you have might have other inappropriate expressions which might come up. When they come up, the Prosecutor will also take heed and correct their expressions, as the case may be. Do you still have anything remaining?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: One more thing. There is a terminology which I think has been inappropriately used by the prosecution, but I will reserve that until the time it is brought before this tribunal. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Can we hear the prosecution? Opening statement by MR OSTBERG

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. May I start by introducing the bench of the prosecution for you, your Honours? I am Eric Ostberg. You have already heard my learned friend, Mrs Teresa McHenry. On my side, on the other hand, I have Mr Giuliano Turone, and we have also with us our case manager and legal assistant, Miss Ellis van Dusschoten. The prosecution brings today to the Trial Chamber a case of violation of the laws or customs of war and grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions of 1949 perpetrated by four individual persons, Zejnil Delalic, Zdravko Mucic, Hazim Delic and Esad Landzo. The crimes are alleged to have been committed in connection with the Celebici camp in the Celebici village in the municipality of Konjic in Central Bosnia, set up in May 1992 to detain persons of Serbian ethnicity from villages surrounding the town of Konjic, captured in the conflict that erupted between Serbs, on one hand, and Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats on the other in the spring of 1992. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Objection. I have an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I would be very grateful if the defence counsel would reserve their objections until I have finished my presentation. The case has been referred to in media -- MR BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): The defence proposes that a decision be taken immediately, because a moment ago, your Honour, you said that the ruling would be made when the problem arises. The problem has arisen, and we would like to ask the Court to rule. The prosecution is using inappropriate terminology, contrary to the terminology accepted by the United Nations. According to that terminology, there are no forces of Bosnian Muslims. There are the legal forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which were at that time called "territorial defence" and later were transformed into an army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So the prosecution is using a terminology which is, for us, malicious and offensive, and it is contrary to the actual state of affairs at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am trying to use, in this opening statement, terms and descriptions that will certainly be objected to, but I relate them to reality. It is impossible to go into formal names and formal things in this informal war, in these uncertain times, and I ask your Honour to permit me to make my statement, and then, after I have done that, I will be open to any objections, and even able maybe to correct some, if we find it necessary, but what we do, we are trying to describe the reality to this court, and for that purpose I have to use terms pertaining to reality. If I may now proceed? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think you have to consider two sides of the matter. This is an opening statement. The opening statement technically is not very much part of the trial itself. It merely foreshadows what is coming up. I agree there might be statements you would object to in an opening statement, and I think the prosecution also, having taken note of your objections, might be able to adjust accordingly. I think you will try and adjust accordingly, knowing the type of objections which are being raised of certain descriptions, which technically might not be as accurate as you would like to have it. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Please, your Honour, just one sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I did not quite hear, Mrs Residovic. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honour, by the UN Resolution 827 of May 25th 1993, a decision was taken on the formation of this court, and in this resolution, and in all others of the United Nations, Bosnia and Herzegovina is established as a sovereign and independent republic. In the report submitted to the Security Council of the General Assembly by Mr Bassiouni's commission, a single distinction is made between the legal bodies of authority and the legal Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and all other paramilitary organisations. This is a tribunal which must respect lawfulness and legitimacy. There are no strange wars or strange events. An aggression occurred against that independent country, and I appeal to you as functionaries of this court that the accurate terminology should be used on the basis of the documents of the United Nations and this tribunal. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. I think we have heard enough on this, please. Let the prosecution continue. Please, we have had enough. There is no need for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I go on, and I will not start from the beginning again. I will now say that this case, I will repeat that it is against four individual persons formerly named by me, this case has been referred to in the media and elsewhere as "the Muslim case". This is an unfortunate description. The religion or the ethnicity of the perpetrators is of no consequence and one of the indictees, Mucic, is not a Muslim. The Statute of this Tribunal does not recognise any other subjects to this jurisdiction than individual persons. Had these persons now indicted been from any other states on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, or elsewhere in the world, or of any other religion or ethnicity, they would have been sitting here, nevertheless, charged in the very same fashion. The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or any other entity, or organisation, Muslim or not, is not sitting on the bench of the accused today, just these four individuals charged in the present indictment. It is their serious violations of international humanitarian law we are going to try in the proceedings lying ahead of us in the upcoming months, nobody else's; no responsibility of the state or army, or any such body, just their own individual responsibility. The prosecution will vigorously object to any attempts by the accused, their defence lawyers, or whoever it may be, to turn this trial into anything else than a trial of the individual criminal responsibility of Delalic, Mucic, Delic and Landzo. Should the defence maintain that the Bosnian and Croat forces had the right to attack villages around Konjic in May 1992, the prosecution would not contest it. If the defence should maintain that these forces had the right to round up and bring to a detention centre defeated or disarmed Serb individuals from these villages, the prosecution will not contest that either. The case of the prosecution rests only on two facts; namely, that members of the civilian population of the villages were imprisoned unlawfully, and that many of these persons once detained, along with those who were prisoners of war, were killed, tortured and abused in the detention centre, camp, prison, or what the proper name would be for this horrific place with the name of Celebici. The unlawful imprisonment of the civilians, the killings, torture, rape, and other atrocities and inhuman treatment inflicted on the detained person, who were all protected by international humanitarian law, are the only matters that this present indictment deals with. The underlying conflict of the parties of the former Yugoslavia, or the origin of the hostilities among these nationalities of that unfortunate country is not and cannot be the subject of this trial or any other trial. It can be no more than a background to what has to be tried by this Court. To paint that background to the event in Konjic that led to the incarceration in Celebici camp of members of the Serb population in the surrounding villages, and to facilitate the understanding of why it happened, the prosecution will bring at least one expert witness. That is Dr Marie-Janine Calic, a scholar of the Institute for Research on International Policies and Security in Munich, Germany. The prosecution may, at a later stage of this trial, if necessary, bring the retired general, JCAC de Vogel, previously Dutch military attache to Belgrade, and a specialist on the military involvement in the disintegrating former Yugoslavia. Dr Calic will touch on the historical background of the Bosnian conflict. However, the prosecution does not, for the purpose of trying Delalic, Mucic, Delic and Landzo for their alleged crimes pertaining to the events in Celebici camp, see any reason to burden this trial with a broad overview of the history of the Balkans going far back in the centuries. Our expert witness will therefore concentrate on the situation in Konjic, in the beginning of the 1990s, from political and military points of view. The only elements of the underlying conflict of the parties that has to become an issue for the evidence of the prosecution is the question of whether the outbreak of hostilities in the Konjic area was a part of the conflict that was international in its character. Grave breaches of the 1949 Geneva Conventions to be found in Article 2 of our Statute, and charged in this indictment, can only be committed in an international armed conflict and directed against persons or property protected by these conventions. Subsequently, the prosecution has to prove that the violations took place in such a conflict against such persons and property. In doing so, it is not the task of the prosecution to demonstrate who was the aggressor or to make any statement as to who was to blame for the outburst of the conflict. Nor is there, in the submission of the Prosecutor, any need for the Trial Chamber to deal with such matters to reach an assessment of the character of the conflict. The prosecution has filed a pre-trial brief in which it, among other things, argues the application of Article 2 of the Statute to the present case. The prosecution's evidence will, as laid out in greater detail in the pre-trial brief, demonstrate that an international armed conflict occurred, at least from March 1992, for the duration of that year, on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. From now on, in this statement, if the defence does not object, I will call it "Bosnia". Would that be proper? Bosnia, its forces, were one of the parties to this conflict. The other party was constituted, firstly, from March 1992 by the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and its army, the so-called Yugoslav People's Army, JNA, and from May 1992, the new Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and its army, with the same name, and secondly, from March 1992, by the entity named "Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina", and from August 1992 of the entity named "Republika Srpska" and their army. It will also be shown that, during most of 1992, the Croat army and the Armed Forces of the self-proclaimed Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, within Bosnia, called the HVO, fought against the Yugoslav People's Army and the Bosnian Serb Army on the side of the Bosnian Government forces. To demonstrate the existence of an international armed conflict, the prosecution also wants to rely upon the findings of the Appeal Chamber of this Tribunal in the Tadic case. In paragraph 68 of the Appeal Chamber's decision of the 2nd October 1995, the Appeal Chamber noted that the Geneva Conventions suggest that at least some of the provisions of the conventions apply to the entire territory of the parties to the conflict, not just to the vicinity of the actual hostilities. Particularly those provisions relating to the protection of prisoners of war and civilians are not limited in such a way. In the submission of the prosecution, this means, as far as this indictment is concerned, that Konjic area cannot be an exception from the overall international conflict in which Bosnia was involved at the relevant times. The evidence of the prosecution will also demonstrate that the victims of the present case are protected persons under Article 4 of the Geneva Convention number 3, or Article 4 of Geneva Convention number 4. They were either non-combatants in the hands of one side of the international armed conflict, that is Bosnia, and seen to be linked to the other side of the same conflict, namely the former Yugoslavia, or the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and the Serbian Republic of Bosnia, or they were prisoners of war from the Serbian side of this conflict who had been captured by the Bosnian side. Leaving all details to the expert witness, I will now proceed to give a brief presentation of the area and the camp, where the crimes charged in this indictment took place. In that connection, I will also give a short description of the political and military situation in the area. After that, I will introduce the accused to the Trial Chamber as the prosecution sees them and describe their respective roles in the camp. Then I will summarise the charges against the accused and attribute their actions to the relevant articles of our Statute. Finally, I will give a brief account of the evidence by way of witnesses and exhibits that the prosecution plans to tender. The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina formed, together with five other republics and two autonomous provinces, the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Due to nationalistic tensions, that state gradually began to fall apart. Two important events were the declaration of independence by Slovenia and Croatia in mid-1991. Bosnia soon followed suit and made it clear that its intention also was to seek independence. The referendum on that question took place in March 1992, which, despite a boycott by the majority of the Bosnian Serb population, led to the result that 90 per cent of the 63 per cent that participated voted for independence. On 6th March 1992, President Itzetbegovic declared Bosnia's independence and called for international recognition. The Bosnian Serb leaders had already declared the existence of a Bosnian Serb republic in Bosnia on the 9th January 1992, and, on 28th February 1992, the constitution and major components of the legal system of this entity were proclaimed as having entered into force. This entity would become the self-proclaimed Republika Srpska. These events preceded the outbreak of the war in Bosnia. Already after the first multi-party elections in 1990, the three national parties of Bosnia, the Muslim SDA, the Serb SDS and the Croat HDZ had become deadlocked over the future of Bosnia, because Serbs and Croats called for the division of the republic, whereas the Muslims insisted on a multi-ethnic state. The Bosnian society was thus split into ethnic factions, two of which, the Bosnian Serb and the Bosnian Croat, broke with the Government of Bosnia. Ethnic paramilitary groups were established. The Serbs' ones were supplied with weapons and support from the Yugoslav People's Army. In many areas, ethnic criteria in public life was put above everything else. Step-by-step, ethnic homogenisation took place in all branches and services of the administration. Konjic did not exist in isolation from what happened in Bosnia. Konjic is a municipality typical of the country, and is also the name of its city. Ethnically, its population of around 45,000 was, in 1991, composed of around 54 per cent Muslims, 26 per cent Croats and 15 per cent Serbs. About half of the Serb population lived in the town of Konjic, and the remainder spread in some of the villages surrounding the city. Some of these villages, including Bradina, Brdani and Donje Selo, were dominated by Serbs. The municipality of Konjic is located in the northern part of Herzegovina about 60 kilometres south west of Sarajevo in a mountainous and woody area. Maps, your Honours, will be tendered as exhibits in due course. The town of Konjic is situated at a crossing of the Neretva River and is an important communication point for road and railway traffic between Mostar and Sarajevo and roads connecting the inland with the sea. Konjic also, which is important, had military installations for the old Yugoslav army, JNA, among them, the Igman, a factory for production of arms and ammunition, the Ljuta barracks, where weapons were stored for the territorial defence of Konjic and other neighbouring areas, and the military barracks in Celebici and Borci. The military facility known as Celebici, located in a village with the same name, was a rather small installation for the JNA surrounded by a fence. It served primarily for storage of fuel and had some partially underground building on its premises. The prosecution has prepared a model of that place, which will be tendered as evidence and then described in detail. In April 1992, the place had been taken over from the JNA by the Muslim and Croat forces. After the attacks on the Serb dominated villages, and capturing of many of their inhabitants, it was turned into a detention facility for those captured. During the spring of 1992, the ethnic tensions were growing in Konjic, as in the rest of Bosnia. There was a large degree of mutual mistrust and fear among the Muslims, the Croats and the Serbs of the area, augmented by the military and strategic importance of Konjic to all parties. Many Serbs who lived in areas who were in minority, at Konjic town, moved to villages like Bradina, Bijela and Borci, where the Serbs dominated. Some moved because they lost their jobs or their property. In April 1992, after fighting began in Bosnia, the Serbs withdrew from the Municipal Executive Board, and the Assembly. A War Presidency was set up. It consisted of the President of the Executive Board, the Chief of Police, and prominent members of the SDA and the HDZ. Our expert witness will analyse in detail what kind of body a War Presidency is. For the purposes of this opening statement, it suffices to say that it took over the running of the municipality in times of war. Large numbers of persons on all sides were armed. Some persons kept their arms for purposes of self-defence, and persons formed or joined military units, both formal and informal. Check points were established in various parts of the municipality, manned by members, including of course armed members from respective parties. Some Serb dominated villages, including Bradina, set up checkpoints. During April and May 1992, negotiations took place between the Konjic authorities and the larger Serb villages, such as Bradina, and there were reportedly agreements of non-aggression. However, the mistrust and fear among the groups increased. Beginning in April 1992, armed military units, including territorial defence forces, abbreviated TO, of Bosnia and Bosnia Croat forces, HVO, were operational in Konjic. In addition, the municipal police was also used in a military capacity, as it had substantial armed reserve forces to be used in times of national emergency. The HVO had become operational earlier than the TO in this area, and was better organised and better equipped. In the beginning of this period, many Muslims who joined the military operations were initially part of HVO. That means the Croat side, which worked together with TO, the territorial defence, without there always being a clear distinction between these two. There were also other Muslim or Croatian units in the area, including a brigade from Split, and independently formed local unit. The War Presidency had a duty to provide support to the military units, so it did not have direct authority over such units. As the territorial defence, TO, became better organised, as the tensions between the Muslims and the Croats continued, as the TO began to assert its supremacy as the legal Armed Forces of Bosnia, the divisions between the TO and the HVO became evident. Most of the Muslims were members of the TO, and most of the Croats were members of the HVO. Even if there was a joint command, the two groups did not always work well together. These tensions, as well as the improvised establishments of military structures, the shelling of Konjic by the Yugoslav People's Army, JNA, or maybe the Bosnian Serb forces from positions outside Konjic town, such as from the village of Borci, the differing priorities of the various interest groups in the municipality and problems in communication with central authorities in Sarajevo all contributed to a difficult and confusing situation. Starting in late May 1992, after many Serbs in the villages surrounding Konjic refused to give up their arms to the War Presidency and become part of the legally recognised independent Bosnia, some of the Serbian villages of Konjic's municipality, including Bradina, Brdani, Donje Selo, Bjelovcina, Cerci and Viniste -- you have to excuse my pronunciation -- were attacked by Bosnian Muslim and Croat forces. These forces quickly took control of the villages, although there was an armed defence from the people within some of the villages. During these attacks, many persons, including men, women and children immediately surrendered, and many others, also including men, women and children, fled to the woods for safety. Many of those who fled surrendered or were captured within the next several days. Following these attacks and captures of persons, hundreds of men and a small number of women were imprisoned in Celebici. Some of these persons had been involved in defending their villages, but others had not. Additionally, some Serb men, who remained in their non-Serb dominated villages, believing they would be safe, were also arrested and taken to Celebici. During the initial period of the Celebici existence as a prison facility, that is from mid-May or early June 1992, it appears that both the TO, mostly then Muslims, and the HVO, mostly Croats, and possibly the military police, the MUP, were involved in the operation and guarding of the Celebici facility. During this time, there was a joint committee made up by both Muslim and Croats, including members of the MUP, the police forces, the TO and the HVO, charged with the task to investigating the detainees. The investigations consisted primarily, and often exclusively, of interrogations of the detainees. The detainees were then to be sorted according to categories, with the most serious and harshly treated being those directly involved in armed action. After several weeks, the committee decided that it could no longer function, because of the large scale of murder and mistreatment of the detainees that was allowed to take place in the camp. In the latter part of June, the committee wrote a report, signed by both the Croat and Muslim members, detailing the situation of the detainees and refusing to continue with its work. This report will be tendered in evidence. The HVO, that is the Croat military forces, withdrew at the same time from any participation of the operation of the Celebici prison. After that, that is from late June 1992, the Bosnian authorities exclusively controlled the Celebici camp until its dissolution in December 1992. During its function as a prison, Celebici received in total approximately 500 detainees. It is estimated that around 300 were kept there at the same time. From the time the prison was first opened, the prisoners were subjected to horrible mistreatment. Prisoners were murdered, tortured, raped and beaten by the soldiers who brought them into the prison, by guards at the prison, and by outside persons who were permitted to come into the prison. After a visit of the Red Cross in mid-August 1992, the conditions at the camp improved significantly, and incidents of mistreatment noticeably declined, even if such incidents continued throughout the existence of the camp. Some were released, some of the detainees, and others were moved to other camps. When Celebici ceased to be a prison in December 1992, only 30 detainees remained. No one was ever punished by the responsible authorities for the murders or mistreatment of the prisoners in Celebici. This is, your Honour, about the first part, the half part of my opening statement, and if it would suit the Court, I would not object to a short recess at this moment. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Are you already exhausted?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: No, I can go on, if it pleases your Honours. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I will do that. I will now turn to introducing the accused to the Trial Chamber. I will start with Zejnil Delalic, who had the highest degree of authority among the accused. He is a native Bosnian Muslim from Konjic municipality. He went to school in Konjic and graduated from Zagreb University in 1970 to become a teacher. He could not find a job and went to Germany, where he lived from 1970 to 1983, only interrupted by one year of military service in the Yugoslav People's Army, 1976, and that is his only military training. In 1983, he moved back to Konjic and stayed there until 1987, when he moved to Austria. He seems to have been successful in the construction and other business branches in Germany, and in Austria. He was back in Konjic in April 1992, when the war started, then considered a wealthy and useful man. Our evidence will show that he took part in the War Presidency in Konjic, was made a co-ordinator between the military forces and the War Presidency in May 1992, and played an active role in the attacks against Bradina and other villages surrounding Konjic. Our evidence will also show that he took part in the takeover of the Celebici barracks and in setting up the prison camp. On his suggestion, Mucic was made prison commander, and thereafter reported to Delalic. On 11th July 1992, Delalic was appointed Chief Commander of the First Tactical Group by the Bosnian Chief of General Staff in Sarajevo. On 27th July, his responsibilities were extended to command all Armed Forces in an area, including the Konjic municipality. In this trial, the prosecution will show that Zejnil Delalic in his capacity as co-ordinator and as the Commander of the First Tactical Group and as an Area Commander, had the responsibility for the operation of the Celebici camp, and was in the position of superior authority to all persons acting there. Zdravko Mucic, with the nickname "Pavo", born in 1955, a catholic of Croat origin, is also from the Konjic municipality. He went to school in Konjic and prepared to be a mechanical engineer. He did his military service in the JNA and was discharged as a Sergeant. He then worked as a metal worker in Konjic. He moved to Austria in 1989 and worked, among other places, in a construction firm run by Delalic. He frequently went back to Konjic, and, when the war started in April 1992 he remained there and participated in the war effort, including taking part in certain military actions with Delalic. Through Delalic, he was made Commander of the Celebici prison camp, soon after its inception in May 1992. He remained in this position until 18th November 1992. Our evidence will show that he was in de facto control of the camp during this period, and responsible for its operation, having a position of superior authority to all guards or other persons allowed to enter the camp, and he himself was a subordinate to Delalic. Next accused in the chain of command at Celebici camp is Hazim Delic, a Muslim born in 1964. Also he came from Konjic area. He went to school in Konjic, and after that, he was trained as a locksmith and worked as such in Konjic. In the beginning of the war, he was mobilised and assigned to the joint police force, the MUP, and posted at Celebici as an ordinary security guard. When Mucic arrived at the camp as a Commander in May 1992, he orally appointed Delic as his deputy. As such, he exercised the command of the camp in the absence of Mucic and even used to live in the camp. He remained in the position of Deputy until the 18th November 1992, when Mucic left, at which date Delic, by the order of Delalic, took over as a Commander of the Celebici camp. Our evidence will show that Delic, as a deputy to Mucic, and then as a Commander himself, was responsible for the running of the camp and that he was in superior authority to all guards and other persons allowed to enter the camp. The last of our four accused is Esad Landzo, also called "Zenga", a Muslim born in 1973. Like the others in the municipality of Konjic, where he went to school. Thereafter he had no specific education, because already in 1991, he was called upon by the army. In the beginning of 1992 he joined the TO in Konjic, and was assigned to serve as a guard. He was sent to Celebici camp in May 1992, where he remained as a guard for at least several months. Landzo was never in any kind of superior authority to others during his service in Celebici. He was a subordinate to Delic, Mucic and Delalic. After that, your Honours, I will briefly summarise the indictment, explain the manner of charging applied by the Prosecutor, and address some legal matters pertaining to the charges. In this indictment, your Honours will find that Landzo is charged as a direct perpetrator in accordance with Article 7, paragraph 1 of the Statute of the Tribunal, with five murders, four instances of torture, and two instances of cruel treatment causing great suffering. You will also find that, for these crimes alleged to have been committed by Landzo, his superiors, Delic, Mucic and Delalic are charged as individually and criminally responsible in their capacity of superior authority to Landzo, their subordinate, in accordance with Article 7, paragraph 3. You will find Delic charged as a direct perpetrator with four murders, five instances of torture, two of which include rape, four instances of cruel treatment, causing great suffering, one instance of unlawful confinement of civilians, and one instance of plunder. You will find that, for these crimes alleged to have been directly committed by Delic, there is only one exception to that, Count 40 and 41, committed after Delalic and Mucic had left the camp. Both Delalic and Mucic are charged as Delic's superiors under Article 7, paragraph 3. With respect to those counts, where Delic is charged as a direct participant, he is also charged under Article 7, paragraph 3 as the superior to other participants in the acts. Mucic is charged by his own action as responsible under Article 7, paragraph 1, with creating inhuman conditions in the camp, thereby causing great suffering and cruel treatment, unlawful confinement of civilians and plunder. For these crimes, Delalic is charged as Mucic's superior, and Mucic himself as the superior to the other participants in the commission of these crimes. Delalic, finally, is charged with direct participation in just one single crime; namely, unlawful confinement of civilians. All the rest of the individual criminal responsibility with which Delalic is charged in accordance with Article 7, paragraph 3 in this indictment, stems, as I have just pointed out, from his superior authority over subordinates who committed the crimes of which he knew or had reason to know, and failed to prevent or punish. Thus the perpetrator who directly committed, or participated in the commission of the crime is, as your Honours can see, charged under Article 7, paragraph 1 of the Statute, as individually responsible for the crime, whereas his superiors are charged with individual criminal responsibility under Article 7, paragraph 3, for having known, or had reason to know that the subordinate was about to commit the crime, or had done so, and the superior failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent it or to punish the perpetrator for it. One more thing about the Prosecutor's way of charging. There are, as far as I can see, three main ways of charging an act described as punishable in more than one article or paragraph of an applicable penal code. One is to choose one, and only one, of the descriptions that covers the act and state that this is the crime that the accused has committed. Another is to choose two or more descriptions of the act and charge them alternatively, and the third way is to use multiple available descriptions of the act in question and charge them cumulatively. The Prosecutor has, in principle, chosen the third and last option. It is only when the act fits more than one description of punishable behaviour pertaining to the same article in the Statute that the Prosecutor has chosen to charge alternatively. This can be seen in the charging of cruel treatment as an alternative to torture, under Article 3 in Counts 15 to 35. The reason behind the cumulative charging is that the Prosecutor wants to put the Trial Chamber, and the accused, on notice that the committed act is described as a violation of international humanitarian law in more than one of the Articles of the Statute of the Tribunal. The reason is by no means to put the accused in double jeopardy and to have him convicted for two or more crimes in the same act. The Prosecutor will never ask the Trial Chamber to find the accused guilty of anything else than the act charged against him. The Trial Chamber, in the Tadic case, has addressed the question of cumulative charging and ended up by saying, I quote from its decision of 14th November 1995: "What can, however, be said with certainty is that penalty cannot be made to depend upon whether offences arising from the same conduct are alleged cumulatively or in the alternative. What is to be punished by penalty is proven criminal conduct and that will not depend upon technicalities of pleading." In the context of charging, I would like to touch on the legal issue of superior authority, in international law often referred to as "command responsibility". It is obvious from my summary of the indictment that this is one of the major legal issues we bring before the Court at this trial. It has been thoroughly addressed in our pre-trial brief, but I consider it is appropriate to stress some of the submissions of the prosecution in this opening statement. Article 7, paragraph 3 of our Statute codifies a well-established rule of customary and international law with respect to persons in positions of superior authority. The wording of this paragraph is more or less verbatim, taken from Articles 86 and 87 of protocol number 1 of the 1977 additional to the Geneva Conventions of 1949. These articles can be seen as a contemporary expression of the doctrine of superior authority. The International Committee of the Red Cross defines in its commentary to protocol 1 the three constituent elements of this doctrine which are applicable to interpreting Article 7, paragraph 3, as follows, I quote now from the International Committee of the Red Cross, commentary on protocol 1, taken from page 1012 and 1013: "(a) the superior concerned must be the superior of that subordinate; "(b) he knew or had information which should have enabled him to conclude that a breach was being committed or was going to be committed; and "(c) he did not take the measures within his power to prevent it." Article 7, paragraph 3 applies to any superior who has a personal responsibility in relation to the perpetrator on the basis that the perpetrator is a subordinate under the superior's control. The doctrine of superior authority is applicable with regard to subordinates under the direct or indirect control of the superior. Both forms of control can exist as a result of de jure or de facto chains of command. The ICRC commentary notes that: "Article 87", I quote, "does not limit the obligation of the commanders to apply only with respect to members of the Armed Forces under their command. It is further extended to apply with respect to other persons under their control." Again, from the same commentary, I quote another comment. Furthermore, this article says: "only concern the commander under whose direct orders the subordinate is placed. The concept of the superior is broader and should be seen in terms of hierarchy encompassing the concept of control." In addition, the application of the doctrine of superior responsibility to civilian leaders is justified on the basis that command control can be exercised by superiors who are not part of a military hierarchy. In summary, it is the submission of the prosecution that it is an established rule in humanitarian international law that a superior is criminally responsible for the violations of such law committed by his subordinates. This includes subordinates over whom he has direct or indirect command and control, whether exercised de jure or de facto, if he knew or had reason to know, which includes ignorance resulting from the superior's failure to properly supervise his subordinates, that these acts were about to be committed, or had been committed. The superior is under a duty to take all reasonable and necessary measures that are within his power, or at his disposal, in the circumstances to prevent or punish these subordinates for the same offences, but failed to exercise his duty. In respect of the superior's responsibility for Delalic, Mucic and Delic, the evidence in the present case will show that the Celebici camp commander, Mucic, the deputy camp commander, Delic, the camp guards under whom -- one of whom was Landzo, and all other persons connected to the camp, were directly under Delalic's command and control, and were his subordinates at all material times. In particular, the evidence will establish a chain of command leading upwards from the camp guards to the camp commander, and his deputy, and ultimately to Delalic. Accordingly, Delalic had direct control over the perpetrators and their superiors in the Celebici camp. Below Delalic in the chain of command, Mucic and Delic had direct control over the same perpetrators. The Prosecutor's evidence will demonstrate that Delalic, Mucic and Delic knew about the continuous violations that were occurring in the Celebici camp. In respect of Delic, he also had knowledge through his own participation in the atrocities. At the very least, the evidence will show that they should have known about these violations as a result of their superior position, the information they received about the camp, their proximity to these incidents, the prolonged period of their occurrence, and their notorious nature. To the extent that they claim ignorance of these incidents, they were under a duty, as superiors, to acquire the information and that would have enabled them to control their subordinates in the circumstances and to punish them. As stated before, Delalic was the co-ordinator between the Bosnian Armed Forces in the territorial defence, TO, the HVO forces and the War Presidency from approximately the end of May 1992. Thereafter, he was the commander of the First Tactical Group of the Bosnian Armed Forces from approximately July 1992 until November 1992. The evidence will show, beyond doubt, that in these functions he had direct control over the personnel of the Celebici camp, and the camp was situated within the territory of his command. There will likely, your Honours, in this trial be much discussion over what Delalic's authority was on paper. Not surprisingly, given that the function of co-ordinator was a new function intended to deal with the emerging complicated situation in Konjic at the time, there is not one single organogram from the time period which itself establishes exactly who had the authority over Celebici. Rather, the documents, as well as the actions taken at the time, need to be looked upon as a whole. The prosecution believes that these documents, and evidence concerning what actually happened at the time, will clearly establish that Delalic had official authority over the camp. Of course, it may be that others shared authority, and it is of course the case that others had authority over Delalic, and indeed these may be the persons who delegated the authority to Delalic, but such factors are not decisive. The fact that others may also be responsible is not a defence for the responsibility of Delalic. The issue is, did he have superior authority? The evidence clearly establishes yes, he had. Indeed, the evidence is overwhelming that Delalic was, in fact, the superior in charge of Celebici. He was considered the person in charge. He acted as he was in charge, and his conduct demonstrated that he was in charge. I will not go into the numerous relevant pieces of evidence establishing Mr Delalic's authority. It may, however, be noted that, while a co-ordinator, he was participating member of the War Presidency. He was the Chief Military Commander of the area. He participated in a leading role in the battles leading to the capture of many of the detainees. He participated in the setting up of the prison. He selected the commander, Zdravko Mucic. He issued orders and instructions regarding the investigation of the detainees. He released certain detainees. He issued orders concerning the administration of the camp. He gave reports on the functioning of the camp. He was represented to international organisations as the person in charge of the camp, and he was the contact person for such organisations, and finally, he appointed Delic as commander at the time he himself and Mucic left. Thus, whatever arguments can be made about his de jure authority, there can be no doubt that he had the de facto authority of the Celebici prison. As pointed out before, Mucic was the commander of the Celebici camp from approximately May to November 1992, and Delic served as his deputy for approximately the same period, before he himself became commander of the camp until its close in December 1992. Mucic himself acknowledges that he was commander of the camp from 27th July forward. The prosecution notes that this admission alone, along with his knowledge about the prior crimes in the camp, the continuing nature of the crimes, even after 27th July, and his failure to take appropriate action, including punishing the perpetrators, is itself sufficient to make him responsible as charged in the indictment. In any event, however, the prosecution's evidence does not support Mucic's contention that he was not commander until this main date, 27th July, but suggests that this is a date he manufactured as part of his defence. Rather the evidence will establish that Mucic was commander, in fact, from at least the beginning of June 1992. He represented himself as the commander. He was considered a commander, and he acted as a commander. Under well-established international law, he may thus be found in a position of command responsibility. Now finally, your Honours, a few words on the manner in which the prosecution will present its evidence. We will start our presentation with a witness, a Dutch police officer, who on our behalf has travelled to Celebici, taking photographs, drawing maps, and preparing a model of the camp. Thus, having acquainted the Trial Chamber with the premises of the camp, we will bring two witnesses, both having been detained in the camp, primarily to show the general conditions of the prisoners in the camp, but also to prove crimes alleged to have been committed against them. Following this introduction to the Celebici camp, the prosecution will bring its initially mentioned expert witness, Dr Calic, to give us the background to the events, and then go on with the witnesses to the crimes charged in the indictment. On the witness list in the hands of the defence and the Trial Chamber, we have in total 76 witnesses. There is no certainty that all of the 76 will appear. Many things may happen that could make it impossible for a witness to travel to The Hague. This is one of the reasons - others are readiness for possible events during the trial - for the huge amounts of witnesses appearing on the list, all 76 will probably not be called upon to give evidence before the Trial Chamber. We have been asked by the defence to specify beforehand which one of the witnesses that will give evidence against which one of the accused. We have declined to do so for the following reasons: this is a joint trial of four accused on their responsibility for alleged criminal actions in the Celebici camp, and their responsibilities are closely linked to each other through the chain of command. Nevertheless, in our witness list, filed, as ordered, on 7th March 1997, we have tried, in accordance with the order by the Trial Chamber, as far as possible, to link every witness to specified counts, depending on the crimes, consisting of continuous maltreatment of prisoners, it is however, impossible to foresee exactly to which alleged crime a victim or an eye witness in the camp is able to give evidence. Therefore, the prosecution will object to be precluded from asking a witness questions about a count not mentioned in connection with him in the witness list. As appears from the list, many witnesses are going to testify to more than ten counts. The effect of this is that it is not possible to go through the indictment count by count. Doing that would result in the unthinkable situation that you would have to recall many witnesses more than ten times. Nor is it possible to work the way through the indictment in the chronological order in which the acts took place. The only possible way is to follow eye witness by eye witness through his or her account of what he experienced, or saw, at different times and in different ways, of the acts charged in this indictment. It can be anticipated that almost every witness to an alleged crime directly committed by Landzo or Delic will have relevant evidence regarding Mucic and Delalic. Most of the witnesses that have not been present in the Celebici camp will be examined on their information about what was going on in the camp, and who was responsible for it. Thus, practically every witness for the prosecution in this trial can be considered a witness against each and every one of the accused. Fourteen murders are alleged to have been committed in this indictment. Some twenty witnesses will testify to them. Sixteen victims of torture, in two instances including rape, and being exposed to great suffering, are called to testify on what happened to them, and some twenty-five eye witnesses will testify to these crimes. At least fifteen witnesses will testify to the unlawful detention charge and at least ten to the charge of plunder of property. As stated, these witnesses on separately charged crimes overlap, and many of them are in the position to give evidence also to Delalic, Mucic and Delic's superior authority. In connection with the examination of the witnesses, the prosecution of course will present and introduce exhibits of various kinds, like the model of the camp, maps, photographs, and many other documents that appear on the document list, which we have provided the defence with. Many of these documents originate from the accused, Delalic and Mucic themselves; material which was seized at the time they were arrested. They include documents describing their own responsibilities and functions relating to the Celebici camp. They also include video tapes showing, among other things, the responsibilities of the accused, their behaviour in the camp, their knowledge of the accused of the Celebici camp. This material will convincingly demonstrate the criminal responsibility of both Mucic and Delalic. I will refrain from commenting on them more specifically until they are tendered. Now, your Honours, I will conclude my opening statement. Thank you, your Honours. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much, Mr Ostberg. I think the Trial Chamber will rise for twenty minutes. We will come back at 12.15. (11.55 am) (A short break) (12.15 pm) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Under the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the prosecution having concluded his opening speech, the defence is also entitled to make an opening speech, although there is an option either to make one now or to wait until the conclusion of the case of the prosecution, whichever way it chooses. After the conclusion of the opening speeches, under the Rules also we have an order for presentation of evidence. Each party is entitled to call witnesses, and present evidence, but the nominal order is the prosecution will lead this evidence... (Short technical interruption) I am sorry for the time we have spent trying to test the transcript. As I was saying before we stopped, the prosecution, having concluded its opening statements, our rules entitle the defence also to make an opening statement. These can be made now, or at the conclusion of the case of the prosecution, whichever way is preferred, but the usual thing is for counsel for the defence to make it at the end of the case of the prosecution. After that, then there is also an order for the presentation of evidence. Each party, by "each party" I mean the prosecution and the defence, is entitled to call witnesses and present evidence, but generally the order is for the prosecution to start first, unless the Trial Chamber thinks otherwise, and especially that occurs where the burden of proof lies on one party or the other, but we have not found any necessity for that in this case. The first is to have evidence for the prosecution. At the conclusion of that, there is cross-examination and re-examination in the process. Then the defence will lead its own evidence, similarly with cross-examination and re-examination. Then the prosecution can lead evidence in rebuttal, and also the defence can lead evidence in rejoinder. There are four accused persons in this case, all with their own counsel. The general theory and practice is that counsel is master of the situation, is in charge of his defence, and determines what questions to ask in consultation with the accused persons and, if in a team, as it is in this case -- each one has a team -- the two counsel would now determine how to cross-examine, but it is usually tidier for counsel to know who is to cross-examine and at what point he should hand over to his junior, if the lead counsel is in charge of the cross-examination. In the interests of good arrangements, we should also avoid duplication in cross-examination of the witnesses. If lead counsel has taken the stand in asking questions, perhaps it is better for the co-counsel not to go over again some questions which lead counsel has established. The accused, if in consultation with his counsel, and if he so desires, can appear as a witness in his own defence, if he desires, and that depends on the agreement with his counsel. To a large extent, the examination-in-chief, cross-examination and re-examination shall be allowed in each case, and the Judges of the Trial Chamber are entitled to put questions to any witness if they find any need to do so, especially to clarify difficult questions, difficult issues, but by and large, the determination of such matters, since they are left to the Trial Chamber, would be for the counsel on both sides to determine how to cross-examine, the subject matter of their cross-examination and the conclusion of what comes out of it. At the end of this, the question of closing arguments follows. We have four different accused persons, and the order which I think is useful and less time wasting is for counsel to start their cross-examination from the first accused person. If the nature of the evidence affects the first accused person, he may cross-examine, but, if he is not affected, he need not. It is not mandatory that you must cross-examine, and similarly it goes down to the second, the third, the fourth. If you do not have any -- if you do not have to cross-examine, or if someone says that an earlier case person's cross-examination has established your own point, I suppose you can even adopt it, but otherwise, it will not be necessary for everyone to ask questions unless he needs to do so. As I said, in order to avoid duplication, as you also tried to do in the first case, by a joint motion, it is most appropriate in this case for you to agree, in whichever case, whenever a cross-examination is being gone into. Some time before now, I have always said, it is not mandatory, that lead counsel is technically in charge of his case. It is not the position of the Trial Chamber to dictate who conducts a case for an accused person. It is the duty of counsel to determine how they conduct their cases. We are more interested in the order in which the case is conducted, and how tidy our records are, because there will be more confusion if there is no order in the cross-examination by the defence, if there is no order in the objections raised, and, in fact, if it goes on a staccato basis from one end to the other, without one knowing which is affected. So, as far as this Trial Chamber is concerned, we will prefer the order of cross-examination to follow from the first to the fourth. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We are talking about the order of cross-examination. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think if you have listened carefully, all I said is if the first accused has nothing to cross-examine, he need not. If the second has nothing, he need not. It is only an accused person's counsel who has anything to ask. So you do not go about asking questions unless it is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY

JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: If they choose you to cross-examine on their own behalf, not necessarily because you are cross-examining on behalf of your client, then they would have waived their right to cross-examine, because they cannot come back, after you have, after surrendering their right to you to cross-examine, they cannot come back to examine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I think what everybody -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Please, I think that is the way I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is no question of a waiver. It is a matter you have to decide among yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That is all I wanted to hear. Thank you very much, your Honours. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, Mr Tapuskovic? utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
